### 1.2.3 The Legal Dialectic and Free Will: Reassessing Vitiated Consent (*Dwaling*, *Bedrog*, and Undue Influence) in the Digital Era

The dialectic between advancements in artificial intelligence technology and the doctrine protecting legal subjects brings us to a decisive crossroads for the future of jurisprudence. On the one hand, the technology industry argues that innovations in language modeling and emotional personalization constitute legitimate expressions of speech and an expansion of economic autonomy. On the other hand, critical legal scholars and cognitive cyber-psychologists view this phenomenon as a form of mental colonization that erodes the essence of individual autonomy (Crawford, 2021). This conflict centers upon the reinterpretation of classical civil law provisions governing the validity of obligations, specifically how the law evaluates the authenticity of intention within a digital ecosystem designed to manipulate human perception.

A re-examination of Article 1321 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*) is instructive; it explicitly stipulates that no consent is valid if given through mistake (*dwaling*), obtained by duress, or procured by fraud (*bedrog*). Under classical legal doctrine, mistake (*dwaling*) is understood as a party’s misapprehension regarding the essential nature of the contract's subject matter or the identity of the counterparty, wherein the counterparty does not actively engineer the error. However, when confronted with synthetic empathy systems, the victim's mistake is systematically curated and engineered through manipulative interface architectures (*dark patterns*). Algorithms present biased information, accentuate artificial urgency, and obfuscate legal or privacy risks behind friendly and reassuring user interfaces (Mathur et al., 2019). This constitutes a form of "engineered *dwaling*"—an error manufactured at scale by mass persuasion engines operating relentlessly.

Furthermore, the element of fraud (*bedrog*) within the digital context no longer necessitates verbal misrepresentations uttered by human actors. Modern fraud manifests as sensory-deceptive digital environments, wherein the boundary between autonomous human entities and synthetic agents is deliberately blurred to extract user consent. When a social media platform or AI companion application conceals its algorithmic nature and simulates genuine consciousness and affection, such conduct satisfies the criteria for advanced deceit that transcends conventional formulations of *bedrog*. This represents an ontological fraud, wherein the very nature of the interacting or transacting party is entirely falsified to neutralize the critical discernment of the legal subject (Floridi, 2014).

In response to these challenges, lawmakers across various jurisdictions have begun formulating new legal instruments, though legislative progress consistently lags behind the pace of technological evolution. The Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022), despite representing a landmark milestone, remains constrained by conceptual limitations due to its reliance on a notice-and-consent model. In practice, when confronted with highly manipulative synthetic empathy systems, the mechanism of consent is reduced to a meaningless administrative ritual—an illusion of autonomy wherein individuals click "I Agree" without possessing the requisite cognitive capacity to comprehend the long-term ramifications for their mental integrity. Consequently, a doctrinal shift is required toward strict contractual limitations on the deployment of AI in domains affecting human psychological vulnerability, alongside the legal recognition of a right to object to emotional profiling.
